title: Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - Conflicts of Interest
subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: A procurement officer is evaluating proposals for IT software. One of the proposals is from a company where the officer's daughter is the Vice President of Sales. Which of the following best describes this situation?
options: An Organizational Conflict of Interest (OCI)
A Personal Conflict of Interest
Bid-rigging
A breach of the Perfect Tender Rule
questions.explain: A personal conflict of interest arises when a public employee's private interests (such as family connections or personal finances) could improperly influence their official public duties.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Vendor X was hired by an agency to write the technical specifications for a new water treatment facility. Later, the agency issues an RFP to build the facility based on those specs, and Vendor X submits a proposal. This creates:
options: A Personal Conflict of Interest
An Organizational Conflict of Interest
A legally binding Option Contract
An Implied Warranty of Fitness
questions.explain: An Organizational Conflict of Interest (OCI) occurs when a contractor's performance on one government contract compromises its ability to be impartial on another, or gives them an unfair competitive advantage (e.g., writing the specs for a bid they plan to pursue).
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: How can a public agency mitigate an Organizational Conflict of Interest (OCI) when a vendor has overlapping contracts?
options: Require the vendor to offer a 10% discount on the new bid.
Implement an information 'firewall' or require the vendor to formally recuse itself from bidding on related downstream work.
Ask the vendor to sign a waiver ignoring the OCI.
Hire the vendor's competitor as a subcontractor.
questions.explain: OCI mitigation often involves implementing strict informational firewalls to prevent data sharing between different divisions of the vendor's company, or including a contract clause that precludes the vendor from bidding on subsequent related implementations.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: The ethical standard known as the 'Appearance of Impropriety' dictates that a public buyer should:
options: Avoid actions that are explicitly illegal.
Avoid actions that, while not strictly illegal, would cause a reasonable observer to suspect bias or wrongdoing.
Maintain professional attire in the workplace.
Publish all personal bank records to the public.
questions.explain: The 'Appearance of Impropriety' standard means public officials must not only avoid actual wrongdoing, but also any circumstances that would cause a reasonable person to question the integrity, fairness, or impartiality of the public process.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: A purchasing agent owns $50,000 worth of stock in a large software company. The agency is about to evaluate proposals for a new ERP system, and the software company is bidding. The agent should:
options: Evaluate the proposals impartially and keep their stock ownership private.
Disclose the financial interest and recuse themselves from the evaluation process.
Sell the stock to a family member and continue evaluating.
Only evaluate the proposals of the competitor companies.
questions.explain: Having a direct financial interest in a bidding vendor creates a massive personal conflict of interest. The buyer must disclose the conflict and recuse themselves from any part of the solicitation, evaluation, or award process.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: To prevent 'revolving door' conflicts of interest, many public agencies enforce policies regarding 'Former Employee Lobbying.' These policies typically:
options: Forbid former public employees from ever working in the private sector.
Require former employees to surrender their government pensions.
Implement a 'cooling-off period' (e.g., 1-2 years) during which former employees cannot lobby their former agency.
Allow former employees to bid on contracts, but only if they offer a discount.
questions.explain: Revolving door policies generally impose a mandatory cooling-off period, restricting a former public employee from representing a vendor in front of their former agency for a certain time frame (often 1 or 2 years).
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: The practice of 'nepotism' in public procurement most accurately refers to:
options: Favoring out-of-state vendors over local vendors.
Showing favoritism in contract awards to relatives or close friends.
Hiring a competitor's employees to gain proprietary secrets.
A vendor offering gifts to multiple buyers at once.
questions.explain: Nepotism is the practice of those with power or influence favoring relatives or friends, especially by giving them jobs or awarding them public contracts.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: In a formal solicitation, providing a specific vendor with advanced drafts of the RFP to review and comment on before the RFP is released to the general public generally causes what type of issue?
options: A breach of the UCC right to cure
An Organizational Conflict of Interest leading to an unfair competitive advantage
A personal conflict of interest
Bid rotation
questions.explain: Giving one potential bidder advanced access to the solicitation documents gives them an unfair competitive advantage (more time to prepare, ability to influence specs), creating a severe Organizational Conflict of Interest.
